summary: Describes Sieve, a language for filtering email at final delivery, with rules for things like sorting messages into folders or discarding them. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 5228 and RFC 5429.

plainLanguage.summary: Sieve is a set of simple instructions for a mailroom helper, like put letters from Grandma in the happy pile. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: how to write mail filter rules
subtitle: A safe, scriptable language for filtering email at delivery time.

tldr.problem: Mail servers and clients need a way to let users filter their email (sorting to folders, discarding spam) without allowing arbitrary programs that could lock up the server or damage data.
tldr.mechanism: Sieve is a simple, non-Turing-complete language for writing filter scripts. It has no loops or variables, only conditional blocks and a fixed set of tests and actions, so it cannot hang or execute dangerous code.
tldr.outcome: Users can safely write filters that run at mail delivery time, and mail systems can offer filter interfaces without security risk. It was later refined in RFC 5228 and RFC 5429.

today: RFC 3028 was obsoleted by RFC 5228 and RFC 5429, which provide a consolidated and updated specification. However, the core concepts, design, and most of the language have remained stable. RFC 5228 is the current Sieve specification and is widely implemented in mail servers and IMAP implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3028 defines Sieve, a language for filtering email at the moment of final delivery to a mailbox. Unlike full-featured programming languages, Sieve is intentionally simple and safe: it has no loops, no variables, and no ability to call external programs. This design makes it suitable for running on mail servers, including IMAP servers, where untrusted user code must not be able to hang the system or cause data loss.

Sieve scripts are executed at the time the mail system deposits a message into the user's mailbox. The language is meant to be easy for users to work with directly, and simple enough that graphical filter editors can generate scripts automatically. Early experience with filtering systems showed that if filtering is made available and easy to use, many users will adopt it to organize mail from specific senders or mailing lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Sieve is a mail-sorting language that lives on the mail server and runs when mail arrives. It is small and safe on purpose, so that even if someone writes a weird rule, it cannot break anything or cause the server to freeze.

sections.title: Language Design
sections.content:
Sieve scripts consist of a sequence of commands separated by semicolons or curly braces. The language is represented in UTF-8 and is case-insensitive for ASCII tokens. Whitespace and comments (both hash-style and bracketed) are allowed and treated as separators.

Sieve has three kinds of literal data: numbers (which may use K, M, or G suffixes for powers of two), quoted strings, and multi-line text blocks. Strings can contain most characters including control characters, and the language provides a way to escape quotes and backslashes within strings.

The core concept is that commands take arguments, which may be positional, tagged (starting with a colon like :contains), or optional. Commands come in three varieties: tests (which return true or false), actions (which do something to the message), and control structures (like if/elsif/else) that execute blocks of commands based on test results.
sections.plainLanguage: Sieve is written as commands in plain text. It looks a bit like English mixed with symbols. Numbers can say how big or small, words tell it what to check, and blocks in curly braces say what to do if something is true.

sections.title: Tests and Actions
sections.content:
Sieve provides a standard set of tests to examine incoming messages. The header test checks email headers for patterns using three match types: :is (exact match), :contains (substring match), and :matches (wildcard glob). The address test is similar but works only on address-containing headers and can extract the local-part or domain. The size test checks message length with :over or :under arguments. The exists test checks whether specified headers are present. The envelope test examines the SMTP envelope from/to addresses. Boolean tests true and false always succeed or fail, and not, anyof, allof combine other tests with logical operations.

Sieve provides five standard actions: keep (file into the main mailbox, the default), discard (silently delete), redirect (forward to another address), fileinto (file into a specific folder), and reject (send a refusal notice to the sender). Some actions may not be available on all implementations; servers must support keep, discard, and redirect at minimum.

A script that performs no actions takes the implicit keep, meaning the message is filed into the main mailbox anyway. This design prevents mistakes from losing mail unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests are questions like is this from someone, is the subject line big, or does the header say this word. Actions are what to do: keep it, throw it away, send it somewhere else, or tell the sender no thanks. If you do nothing, the mail goes to the inbox anyway so it is not lost.

sections.title: Control Structures and Blocks
sections.content:
Sieve provides conditional execution via if, elsif, and else keywords. An if command takes a test and a block of commands enclosed in curly braces; if the test is true, the block is executed. elsif and else` may follow to provide alternative branches, similar to other programming languages. Because of the grammar, each branch runs zero or one blocks, never multiple blocks.

The require command declares which optional features (capabilities) a script uses. If a required capability is not supported by the server, the entire script is rejected and not executed. This ensures that scripts do not fail partway through.

The stop command ends all processing immediately. If no actions have been executed before stop, the implicit keep happens.

These control structures are the only way to create conditional logic; there are no loops. A script is executed once per arriving message.
sections.plainLanguage: If/else lets you say do this if something is true, or do that otherwise. Require tells the server what optional features your script needs, and stop says stop right here, do not check anything else. No loops, just straight-line logic with branches.

sections.title: Extensibility and Deployment
sections.content:
Sieve scripts are transmitted as plain text files with MIME type application/sieve. The language allows vendors and standards bodies to define new tests, actions, and options through capability strings. A vendor-specific capability begins with vnd. followed by the vendor and product name, such as vnd.acme.rocket-sled. The require statement must declare any non-standard capabilities before the script uses them, and if a required capability is not available, the script fails to load.

The specification defines required messages and options for supporting stateless operation and interaction with DHCP relay agents, allowing straightforward interoperable implementation of clients and servers. Site policies may limit the total number of actions executed or constrain which actions can be used together, for example preventing both reject and fileinto on the same message.
sections.plainLanguage: New filtering features can be added over time without breaking old scripts. If a script asks for a feature the server does not have, the script just will not run. Servers can say no to weird combinations of actions to prevent mail bombs.
